result:
Solution 3 is the only one whose reasoning holds up, and its answer is 1/(2t(t−1)). I checked the upper bound in full but could only partly verify the construction, so I am also relying on this matching a result I recall from the literature.

**Upper bound (Solution 3).** In a K_{2,t+1}-free graph, any two vertices have at most t common neighbors. If u, v lie on side A of a copy K_{t,t} with other side B, then B is contained in N(u)∩N(v), which has at most t vertices, so B = N(u)∩N(v). Thus any pair of vertices lies on a common side of at most one copy. Each copy has 2·C(t,2) = t(t−1) same-side pairs, so there are at most C(n,2)/(t(t−1)) ≈ n²/(2t(t−1)) copies. This argument is correct.

**Construction.** I could not fully verify the algebraic construction on n = t^{2e−1} vertices, but it is plausible. The common-neighborhood count of exactly t checks out. The degree is about n^{1/2}, which is consistent with the K_{2,t+1}-free edge bound. The claim that almost all pairs lie in a K_{t,t} matches the upper bound, which gives the limit 1/(2t(t−1)).

**Why the others fail.**
- Solution 2 claims the number of copies through a vertex v is O(deg v). Pairwise-intersecting-in-at-most-one t-sets inside N(v) can number on the order of deg(v)², not deg(v). So the n^{3/2} bound is unjustified. The construction above shows the true growth is quadratic in n despite only about n^{3/2} edges.
- Solution 1 gives 1/t! with no real derivation. It also conflicts with the proven upper bound 1/(2t(t−1)) for t ≥ 3, since 1/t! is smaller than that bound only by coincidence of form and is not supported by any argument.

CHOICE: 3
